title: Overcome anger by kindness (223–228)
hookLine: overcome anger by not-anger, evil by good, the miser by giving, the liar by truth; no one is never blamed
last: OTHER PEOPLE ARE BUT HOLDING THE REINS.

lines: MATCH THEM, OR THE OTHER MOVE.
cards: Someone is rude to you at the checkout. The obvious move is to match them: a little coldness back, a sigh, maybe a comment. It feels fair.
And then you both walk away a bit worse than you arrived. Now picture the other move. You say, it's been a long day for you, hasn't it, and smile.
Sometimes the other person softens right there. Sometimes they don't. But something in you stays clean either way.
Yesterday was about stopping the chariot; today's verse is about which direction to drive it.

teach.b: Verse two twenty-three, in Max Müller's translation: "Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!"
Four pairs, each fought with the opposite weapon.

Müller wrote love, but the Pali is akkodha, simply non-anger, calm. You don't beat anger by being angrier; you beat it by not joining in. Harm is met with good, stinginess with generosity, lies with truth.
It only works if you refuse the other person's weapon. Then the chapter turns to something that makes this easier: you'll be criticized no matter what.
The commentary tells of a layman named Atula who went with friends to hear a teaching. The first monk they visited sat in silence, and Atula grumbled that he said nothing.
The next, Sāriputta, gave a long, deep teaching, and Atula grumbled that it was too long. The next, Ānanda, spoke briefly: too short.

Finally he went to the Buddha, who told him, in verse two twenty-seven, that this was an old saying: they blame the silent, they blame the talkative, they blame the one who says little, "there is no one on earth who is not blamed."
And verse two twenty-eight: "There never was, there never will be, nor is there now, a man who is always blamed, or a man who is always praised." If blame is guaranteed, you're free.
You might as well answer with kindness.

how: Teachers often turn to verse 223 when they speak about patience, and many Buddhists practice meeting hostility with calm and generosity, often supported by loving-kindness meditation toward difficult people.

o: staying silent so nobody can blame you
non-anger: a calm that refuses to fight back
a fast kept on holy days

games.q: match each problem to its opposite weapon.

s: Müller's 'love' in verse 223 translates akkodha, non-anger
the Pali simply means not-anger, calm.
the verse says to meet anger with a stronger anger
each harm is met with its opposite: anger with non-anger.
verse 228 says some people are always praised
"there never was, there never will be" anyone always blamed or always praised.

games.q: you're Atula. one monk was silent, one spoke long, one spoke briefly, and you grumbled at them all. now you go to the Buddha. what does he tell you?
o: you've finally found the perfect teacher.
no one on earth is not blamed.
games.why: "there is no one on earth who is not blamed." the silent, the talkative and the brief are all blamed: it's an old saying.

practice: Think of someone who has been harsh with you lately, picture their face as neutrally as you can, and notice the urge to match them.
Then, just in your mind, offer the opposite weapon that fits: a kind word for harshness, a small gift for stinginess, a plain truth, gently said, for a lie.
You don't have to do it today; wish them ease for one breath, and let them go.

wordCard.voice: Akkodha. Non-anger, calm: verse two twenty-three says anger is overcome by non-anger, harm by good, the stingy by giving, the liar by truth.

orig.note: Pali: non-anger, calm — akkodhena jine kodhaṃ, overcome anger by non-anger.

carryVoice: Your line: overcome by giving. Four harms, four opposite weapons. Day two hundred two, done.
